This modest initial mass reflects the lecithotrophic strategy of the prolarva, which relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during its first days post-eclosion. The hatching event itself is marked by chorion rupture and the release of a poorly developed, transparent larva that remains largely motionless near the substrate. These non-feeding, mouth-closed larvae gradually absorb their yolk sac over the course of several days before transitioning to exogenous nutrition. The onset of first feeding coincides with mouth opening and the depletion of the remaining yolk reserves, a critical bottleneck that determines early survival rates in this species.

As growth proceeds through the planktonic larval phase, Bagre marinus undergoes a dramatic increase in body size, culminating in an ultimate total length of 69 centimeters [Li = 69 centimeters] for fully mature adults. This asymptotic length is among the largest recorded for ariid catfishes in the Gulf of Mexico, where the species maintains a broad distribution across estuarine and nearshore habitats. The body weight corresponding to this ultimate length is approximately 4,296 grams [Wwi = approximately 4,296 grams], a figure that reflects the robust, laterally compressed body plan typical of the family. Reaching this size typically requires between one and two years in the warm waters of the northern Gulf of Mexico, although local thermal regimes can influence the precise timing. The sub-adult phase is characterized by continued somatic investment alongside the initiation of reproductive physiology. Individuals below this length show no signs of gametogenic activity, and histological examination of their gonads reveals only immature oogonia or spermatogonia. Once the length at puberty is surpassed, both sexes begin preparing for their first spawning event, which usually occurs during the spring and summer months.

Reproductive output in Bagre marinus is relatively low for a teleost of its size, with females producing a single clutch per spawning event.
